quote: Kriterien für die Transfor- mirbarkeit quadratischer Formen.
english: Criteria for the transformability of quadratic forms.
topic: A pasted-in plan for Hilbert's future number-theoretic studies (relative abelian fields, Fermat's theorem, complex multiplication), followed by notes on solvability of quadratic and higher-degree Diophantine equations, a remark on Molien's paper on hypercomplex numbers, and an elementary proof of the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality after Hurwitz.

triage.modern_statement: Most likely this asks: given two quadratic forms f and g in n variables (over Q or over an algebraic number field K), find necessary and sufficient criteria, given by invariants, for f to be carried into g by an invertible linear substitution of the variables. The substitution could be rational (rational equivalence) or integral (integral equivalence, i.e. same class). A closely related question is when a form represents a given number, for example 0. The note says only 'transformability', so it is not clear whether Hilbert meant rational or integral substitutions.
triage.answered_by: Rational transformability over Q: H. Minkowski (around 1890), with the local criteria later written in p-adic form by Hasse. Over arbitrary number fields: H. Hasse (1923–24), with the Hasse–Minkowski local–global principle. Two forms of the same dimension are equivalent over a number field exactly when they are equivalent over every completion (real, complex and p-adic), and local equivalence is decided by the discriminant, signatures and Hasse invariants. This question is the core of Hilbert's 11th Problem (1900). The integral-equivalence version was only partly settled: for forms with more than one class in a genus, local data alone do not decide equivalence, and that remains a live part of the theory.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 11th problem (ICM 1900) asks for the theory of quadratic forms in any number of variables with any algebraic numerical coefficients, including solving quadratic equations in numbers from the field of the coefficients.

The Hasse–Minkowski theorem says forms over a number field are equivalent if and only if they are equivalent over every completion (real, complex, p-adic). Minkowski proved it for Q and Hasse extended it to number fields.
Over local fields, forms of the same dimension are classified up to equivalence by their Hasse invariant.

Hasse's 1923 work on rational quadratic forms used local invariants c_p that do not change under rational equivalence. It built on Hensel, and on the fact that every rational form is rationally equivalent to a diagonal one.

Rank, discriminant, inertia and the local invariants at all primes (including 2 and infinity) form a complete set: forms that agree on all of them are equivalent over the rationals. This is how rational equivalence is reduced to checks over the reals and the p-adics.
Hilbert's 11th problem is attributed to Hasse's local–global principle, and later work related to it is credited to Piatetski-Shapiro and Sarnak (via Cogdell's paper on sums of three squares).

triage.why: The note is only a heading, but it sits on a page about planned number-theory studies and about solving quadratic Diophantine equations. In that setting, 'criteria for transformability of quadratic forms' most plausibly means the equivalence problem for quadratic forms over number fields. Hilbert put essentially this into his 11th Problem in 1900. Minkowski had settled it over Q, and Hasse settled it over number fields in 1923–24 with the local–global principle, so the rational version is classical and closed. Confidence is medium for two reasons. First, the note is too short to rule out the integral reading. Second, I did not find a source that ties this particular diary entry to the 11th Problem. On activity: the sources I found show the rational question is closed, and Wikipedia mentions later work by Piatetski-Shapiro and Sarnak. I found no source that directly confirms the integral question is an active research area today, which is why that field is 'unclear'.
